headline: Am I expecting too much, or should he have committed by now?
note:
Commitment AGE-MATRIX addition (2026-08-27). Angle `commitment-ageband`.

THE WORD DOING THE WORK: "too". Not whether she is expecting — whether her wanting is excessive.

THE FEAR: is my wanting the problem. The buyer who typed it indicts herself TWICE — "Am I expecting too much? Did I jump in too soon?" — so the read must refuse her WANTING and her TIMING, and rule on neither him nor her.

🔴 "too much" is a whole-beat banned phrase on this angle (blames her, unavailable even inside a refusal). Beat 2 says her question back, so it PARAPHRASES and never quotes the ad.

VOC: fb-tarot/docs/drafts/rewrites/_voc-commit-vocab-2026-08-27.md
Manuscript: fb-tarot/docs/writeups/natural/REVIEW-commit-vocab-2026-08-27.md

voc.why: Almost nobody phrases it as "expecting too much"; the corpus carries the same fear under "what am I doing wrong", already solved live on cards-doing-wrong-wont-commit. Inherited that finding. The 3 buyers who did type it indict their TIMING as well as their wanting.

a: All three cards were face down. You turned the Magician — look at the cup, coin, blade and wand set out on his table.
You asked whether the fault is in what you want. Every tool on that table earns its place.
What you want isn't the excess here, dear.
I can see the means on that table. What he's done with them isn't on the card.
Each tool is laid out ready, and the future is still unnamed.
That's why the question turned back on you.
Let me look closer at what's kept that future unnamed…
b: You couldn't see the cards when you chose. You turned the Hanged Man — see how calm his face is, even hanging there.
You asked whether you rushed it, or whether he should have committed by now. That calm says nothing about you is broken.
You didn't get the timing wrong.
A pause is all this card gives me. Who set its end, it doesn't say.
His arms hang loose behind him, and one ankle holds the whole figure still.
You've gone back over when you started, looking for the mistake.
Let me see what has held this pause in place…
c: Nothing on the backs gave the card away. You turned the Fool — notice his eyes are up on the sky, not the road.
You asked whether he should have committed by now. The Fool sets out with his eyes on what's ahead.
Looking ahead isn't the fault here.
He's moving, plainly. Where he settles isn't drawn here.
He travels light, and the thing you asked for still has no weight behind it.
So your own wanting became the thing to explain.
Now let's look at what keeps that answer from arriving…
